proposal.utterance: Classify 'Abusus' (the right of abuse, in Roman-law property theory) in BFO terms.

entities.label: Abusus
entities.rationale: Abusus is a specific kind of legal right recognized within Roman-law property theory: the right of the owner to alienate, consume, or destroy the thing. As a legal right, it is a role (BFO_0000023) borne by a person or legal entity with respect to a thing, grounded externally in the legal-institutional framework rather than in any intrinsic disposition of the bearer. It is best modeled as a subclass of the existing working:LegalRight class (itself typed as BFO_0000023). It is a class (a kind of right) rather than an individual instance.

entities.label: RomanPropertyRight
entities.rationale: Roman-law property theory distinguishes usus, fructus, and abusus as component property rights. A superclass RomanPropertyRight captures the genus of which Abusus is a species. This is needed to correctly situate Abusus in the existing class hierarchy. It too is a Role (BFO_0000023) since property rights are externally grounded social-legal statuses.

entities.label: Usus
entities.rationale: Companion component right (right of use) in the Roman dominium triad; included for structural completeness of the RomanPropertyRight genus. Typed as Role (BFO_0000023).

entities.label: Fructus
entities.rationale: Companion component right (right to fruits/profits) in the Roman dominium triad; included for structural completeness. Typed as Role (BFO_0000023).

relations.rationale: RomanPropertyRight is a species of LegalRight, inheriting its BFO_0000023 typing.
Abusus (right of abuse/alienation/destruction) is one of the three component property rights in the Roman dominium framework, hence a subclass of RomanPropertyRight.
Usus (right of use) is a co-ordinate component of Roman dominium alongside Abusus and Fructus.
Fructus (right to fruits) is a co-ordinate component of Roman dominium alongside Abusus and Usus.

open_questions: Should Abusus be modeled as a class (a kind of right, applicable to any owner in a Roman-law system) or also as a specific individual instance tied to a particular legal corpus (e.g., the Roman Corpus Juris Civilis)? Currently proposed as a class.

Roman dominium (full ownership) is sometimes treated as the whole of which usus, fructus, and abusus are parts. Should we also mint a working:Dominium class (BFO_0000023, LegalRight) and use BFO_0000051 (has part) to relate it to the three component rights? BFO part-of between roles on the same bearer is ontologically non-trivial and may require an open question about whether the mereology applies at the role-type level.
Should RomanPropertyRight, Usus, and Fructus be committed to the ontology at this time, or only Abusus as requested? The companion classes are proposed for structural coherence but can be deferred.

Is the bearer of Abusus restricted to a natural person (BFO_0000040 material entity, specifically a human organism) or also to a legal person (a collective/corporate entity)? This affects how the inheres-in relation should be scoped.
proposal.rationale_summary: Abusus, the Roman-law right of abuse (encompassing the powers to alienate, consume, transform, or destroy a thing), is most accurately typed in BFO as a Role (BFO_0000023): it is a specifically dependent continuant that inheres in the owner of a thing, is externally grounded in the Roman legal-institutional framework, and can be realized in processes of alienation or destruction. Because the existing working ontology already has working:LegalRight as a subclass of BFO_0000023, Abusus is naturally a subclass of LegalRight. To situate it within Roman property theory specifically, an intermediate class working:RomanPropertyRight is proposed as the genus, with Abusus, Usus, and Fructus as coordinate species—mirroring the classical tripartite analysis of dominium. All three sibling classes are Roles (externally grounded legal statuses) for the same reasons as LegalRight. The main open questions concern whether mereological structure should be encoded between Dominium and its component rights, whether companion classes Usus and Fructus are in scope, and whether the bearer should be restricted to natural or also legal persons.
